intro: This guide takes your group through Praying Hyde (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It’s written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. It tells the story of John Hyde, a shy, increasingly deaf American missionary in the Punjab who became known as “the man who never sleeps” because of his praying, and it is careful to separate what the records show from the legends that grew up around him.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close in prayer (2–3 minutes), in your own words or by turning the chapter’s closing “One thing to do this week” into a prayer together, and leave that challenge with the group for the week ahead.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself first and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. The book is about prayer, but it also deals with pride, besetting sin, a young man’s struggle with drink, the cruelty of caste, and Hyde’s neglect of his own sleep and food, which harmed his health before he died of a tumour. Keep all reflection on personal sin private, as the activities do, and never ask teens to confess anything in front of the group. Chapter 12 says plainly that rest, food and sleep are God’s gifts, so watch for anyone who seems to be punishing their body or caught in an addiction, follow up gently, and point them to a parent, pastor, doctor or other trusted adult.

weeks.summary: John Hyde grows up in a minister’s home where his father prays again and again that the Lord will “thrust out laborers” into his harvest. After his older brother Edmund dies, John carries the question of going abroad for most of a year, settles it on his knees, and sails for the Punjab in 1892, later admitting that “self” was at the foundation of his ambition. The big idea: God doesn’t wait for our motives to be pure before he sends us; he purifies them on the way.

memory_verse.text: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.

activity.title: Settle It on Your Knees
steps: Ask the group how people usually make big decisions: asking friends, lists of pros and cons, searching online, praying.
Reread the part where Hyde’s classmate refuses to give him more arguments and sends him to pray, and discuss why.
Have each person write down privately one question about their future they keep going round in circles about.
Give everyone three minutes of silence, phones away, to bring that question to God.
Talk about the chapter’s point that mixed motives are normal, and that God can purify them on the way.

weeks.summary: Boarding his ship, Hyde finds a letter from a friend of his father promising to pray until he is filled with the Holy Spirit, and in his pride he crushes it and throws it aside. After days of struggle he smooths it out, asks God to fill him, sees his selfish ambition, and becomes willing to be a missionary working quietly out of sight. The big idea: some hard words come from people who love us, and the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

memory_verse.text: If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

activity.title: Bin It or Smooth It?
steps: Read out several sample criticisms, some fair and caring and some careless or unkind, such as “You never listen when people disagree with you” or “You’ll never be any good at this.”
For each one, have the group decide whether it belongs in the bin or should be smoothed out and taken seriously, and why.
Discuss how you can tell when a hard word is one of the “wounds of a friend.”
Have each person think privately of one criticism they brushed off recently and ask themselves whether any part of it is true.

weeks.summary: In his first days in the Punjab, Hyde hears a man ask a preacher whether he himself has been saved from sin, and knows he would have to say no because of one sin that still clings to him. He tells God that either God must give him victory or he will go home, and God assures him he is able and willing to deliver him; years later Hyde is still telling others about his conflicts with sin and God’s help. The big idea: God can break sin’s rule over us, and that freedom is the start of a road, best walked with help.

memory_verse.text: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us.

activity.title: Lay It Aside
steps: Ask a volunteer to walk across the room carrying a heavy bag, then walk back without it, and ask what changed.
Read Hebrews 12:1 and talk about the difference between a “weight” and “sin which clings so closely.”
Discuss why Hyde refused to go on preaching until he could testify to the gospel’s power in his own life.
Give everyone a quiet minute to name their own besetting sin to God silently, keeping it between them and God.
Encourage them to tell one trusted, mature Christian this week and ask for prayer.

weeks.summary: Hyde’s first ten years in India are faithful but not especially fruitful: he is shy, increasingly deaf and slow to answer, and the mission committee rebukes him for putting Bible study before language study. Colleagues disapprove of how much he prays, yet he holds no bitterness, saying, “they did not understand me, that was all, they never intended to be unkind.” The big idea: God doesn’t always remove our weaknesses but works through them, and slow, faithful years can be the soil for what comes next.

memory_verse.text: Who has made man’s mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.

activity.title: Assume the Best
steps: Read out a few everyday situations: a friend doesn’t reply to your message, a teacher marks you down, a parent seems short with you.
For each one, have the group suggest first the worst explanation and then the most generous one.
Reread Hyde’s words about his colleagues and ask what difference assuming the best made to him.
Challenge everyone to try his response the next time they feel misunderstood this week.

weeks.summary: In the caste-bound Punjab the gospel spreads through the poorest villages after a lame hide dealer named Ditt is baptized and brings his family to Christ, and the number of Indian Christians there grows from 3,912 in 1881 to 163,994 in 1911. Hyde works the Moga district with Indian evangelists such as Jalal Masih, embraces low-caste Christians in public and lives with village preachers as a brother. The big idea: God chooses the people the world overlooks, and the gospel ignores the lines we draw between people.

memory_verse.text: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.

activity.title: Map the Lines
steps: In small groups, sketch, without using any names, the unwritten “caste system” of a typical school or town: who sits where, who gets noticed, who gets laughed at.
Discuss what crossing those lines looks like, using Hyde’s public embrace of low-caste Christians as an example.
Talk about why Ditt went home to his relatives instead of moving into the mission compound, and what that meant for his village.
Have each person decide privately on one person who often gets left out, and one way to spend time with them this week.

weeks.summary: After staying up all night to prepare a Bible talk, Hyde wonders whether preparing himself matters as much as preparing the message, and begins nights of prayer that others soon join. In 1904 he helps start the Punjab Prayer Union, whose members promise half an hour of prayer each day around noon for an awakening. The big idea: the messenger needs preparing as much as the message, and a small promise kept daily can outlast a big resolution made once.

memory_verse.text: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God.

activity.title: A Promise You Can Keep
steps: Read the Prayer Union’s promise aloud and ask why half an hour, not all night, was the point.
Discuss why Hyde’s friends warned people not to copy his all-night way of praying.
Have each person write down a realistic daily prayer time for this week, with a fixed time and a length they can actually keep.
Pair up and agree to ask each other next week how it went, without judging.

weeks.summary: At the first Sialkot convention in 1904, after a night arguing with God, Hyde speaks honestly about his own struggles and God’s help, and many others begin to pray. At the 1905 convention he teaches that the Holy Spirit is the true witness to Jesus, and one morning a speaker, almost certainly Hyde, says, “He has given me no message for you to-day,” opening days of conviction, confession and joy. The big idea: in whatever we lead or say, the Holy Spirit should go first, with us behind him.

memory_verse.text: But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.

activity.title: Who Goes First?
steps: Ask the group to list things they lead, play or speak at: a class presentation, a team, a worship band, a conversation with a friend about faith.
For each one, discuss what it looks like to care more about how you come across than about what God is doing.
Read Hyde’s question to the pastors and ask how it might apply to teenagers.
Have each person write down one thing coming up that they will lead or take part in, with the prayer “Holy Spirit, go in front; I’ll stay behind you.”

weeks.summary: Hyde brings a tired Pengwern Jones into the prayer room, then sends him off to speak, saying, “Go in and speak, that is your work,” while he goes back to pray for him. At the Sialkot conventions prayer goes on day and night; Hyde prays face down, repeating “Wide, Lord,” and dances for joy when people find peace with God, though he also neglects meals and sleep. The big idea: praying for others is real work, the hidden half of what God is doing.

memory_verse.text: I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

activity.title: Behind the Scenes
steps: As a group, list the hidden jobs behind a church service, a school play or a sports match.
Discuss why Hyde saw praying and preaching as two halves of one job.
Have each person write the name of someone facing something hard this week, and a time when they will pray for them.
Encourage them to tell that person, “That’s your work; praying for you is mine.”
Point out the chapter’s warning too: even Hyde asked God whether to go to lunch, and went.

weeks.summary: In 1908 Hyde is in deep travail for the people of his district, praying, “Father, give me these souls or I die!” The famous soul-a-day claims rest on one memoir written years later, while the records and Hyde’s own letter show daily baptisms on touring days, shared with his Indian team. Once, after a family of nine is baptized, he refuses to leave until a tenth person, a boy who had been out playing, is found. The big idea: love counts people one by one, not as a score.

memory_verse.text: What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?

activity.title: Legend or Record?
steps: Read out the legend version of Hyde’s soul-a-day story, then the words from his own letter quoted in the chapter.
Ask why the honest version is smaller but still extraordinary, and why the word “us” matters.
Discuss how numbers can turn into a scoreboard, in church, in sport or on social media.
Have each person write privately the name of one person near them whom nobody seems to notice, and pray for them by name each day this week.

weeks.summary: Praying about a pastor whose faith seems to have gone cold, Hyde starts listing his faults and is stopped short, realising he has become an “accuser of the brethren.” He prays instead, “Father, show me what things are lovely and of good report in my brother’s life,” and spends the whole time thanking God for the man, who soon afterwards receives a great spiritual uplift. The big idea: criticism sees people as problems, but thanksgiving sees them as God’s work in progress.

memory_verse.text: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.

activity.title: Three Lovely Things
steps: Ask the group how people sometimes slip into complaining about others, even while “praying for” them.
Read Hyde’s new prayer from the chapter aloud.
Have each person privately choose someone who irritates them and write down three true things about them that are good or worthy of praise.
Give a minute of silence for everyone to thank God for each of the three things, with no “but.”

weeks.summary: A young Brahman known as J. N. confesses Christ, falls into drink, and is taken in by Hyde again and again, even after stealing and selling his clothes. When J. N. leaves on a train, Hyde pleads with him at the window in tears, and the next day J. N. comes back because he could not forget those tears; yet years later his struggle with drink is still not over. The big idea: love doesn’t always fix people, but it can keep them coming back.

memory_verse.text: Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears.

activity.title: No Lecture
steps: Discuss why J. N. came back after the train left, and why one of Hyde’s evangelists found his patience so frustrating.
Talk about the difference between a message that lectures and one that simply says “I care.”
Have each person draft privately a short message, with no lecture in it, to someone who has drifted from God or from them.
Remind the group that if someone they love is caught by drink, drugs or anything like it, they don’t have to carry it alone and can talk to a trusted adult or a helpline.

weeks.summary: After the 1910 Sialkot convention, worn out by sleepless nights and leading meetings with a fever, Hyde sees a doctor in Calcutta who says his heart has shifted to the right side and orders months of quiet. The chapter is careful: this is a friend’s memory of one doctor’s remark, there are medical explanations, and Hyde later died of a tumour; but years of vigils, missed meals and little sleep almost certainly harmed him. The big idea: rest, food and sleep are gifts from God, and Jesus told his tired disciples to come away and rest.

memory_verse.text: And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat.

activity.title: Gifts, Not Weakness
steps: Read Mark 6:31 and ask what it shows about how Jesus treated his tired disciples.
Discuss the difference between Hyde’s spirit of prayer and the form he practised, as his friends described it.
Have each person write down privately one way they tend to neglect rest, sleep or their health.
Ask everyone to choose a time to put their phone away each night this week and write it down.
Remind the group that anyone who feels they must punish their body to be good enough should tell a safe person.

weeks.summary: Seriously ill in Britain, Hyde advises a very deaf old woman to use church to pray for the preacher and the people, and goes to pray for J. Wilbur Chapman’s struggling mission at Shrewsbury, where the tide turns. He dies of a tumour at his sister’s home in Northampton in 1912 after weeks of suffering, saying, “Thank God for pain” and “It’s just victory, victory, victory,” with a Punjabi cry of victory for Jesus as his last words. The big idea: the habits of thanksgiving and prayer we build now are the ones we will have when life gets hard.

memory_verse.text: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

activity.title: Habits for Hard Days
steps: Ask the group to list habits from Hyde’s life across this book, such as giving thanks, praying for others, refusing grudges and carrying burdens.
Discuss why the chapter says nobody learns to say “Thank God for pain” on their deathbed.
Have each person choose one of those habits to practise this week and write it down.
Have them also write the name of one person carrying something heavy, and set a daily reminder to pray for them.
Close by saying the memory verse together as a thank-you to God.
